name: Orion
introduction: is the Hunter, perhaps the most recognizable constellation in the sky: two bright shoulders, two bright knees and three stars in a neat row for a belt. Because it straddles the celestial equator, Orion is visible from every inhabited part of Earth, high in northern winter and southern summer evenings, where it appears upside down.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Orion is a window into a stellar nursery. Most of its belt and sword stars belong to Orion OB1, a family of hot, massive stars born from the giant molecular clouds that still fill this part of the sky. They burn so fiercely that they will live only a few million years, a blink compared with the Sun’s ten billion.

The figure is not flat. [Bellatrix](hip:25336) is about 250 light-years away, [Betelgeuse](hip:27989) about 500, and the middle belt star [Alnilam](hip:26311) nearly 2,000. The Hunter only looks like a single shape from our vantage point; rotate the map and he falls apart.
Orion is also a celestial signpost: follow the belt southeast to Sirius, the brightest star of the night, or northwest past Aldebaran to the Pleiades.

image.caption: Star View schematic · catalogue positions, north up and east left
image.alt: Orion’s three belt stars point southeast to Sirius and northwest to Aldebaran and the Pleiades.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Betelgeuse](hip:27989) is a red supergiant so large that, placed where the Sun is, it would extend beyond the orbit of Mars. In late 2019 and early 2020 it faded dramatically in the “Great Dimming”, when a cloud of dust it had shed briefly veiled part of its surface. It is expected to end as a supernova, most likely within the next hundred thousand years, at a safe distance from Earth.

[Rigel](hip:24436), the blue-white foot, usually outshines Betelgeuse. It is a young supergiant about 860 light-years away, tens of thousands of times more luminous than the Sun, with smaller companion stars.

The belt stars [Alnitak](hip:26727), [Alnilam](hip:26311) and [Mintaka](hip:25930) are blue giants and supergiants. Mintaka sits almost exactly on the celestial equator, so it rises due east and sets due west from anywhere on Earth. [Saiph](hip:27366) marks the second knee, and [Heka](hip:26207), also called Meissa, the Hunter’s head.
Not every star here is a distant giant: [Tabit](hip:22449), in the Hunter’s shield, is a Sun-like star only 26 light-years away, a near neighbor that merely happens to line up with the figure.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Below the belt hangs the sword, whose middle “star” is the [Orion Nebula](id:orion-nebula) (M42), the nearest large region of massive star formation, about 1,350 light-years away and visible to the naked eye as a soft glow. At its heart, four young stars called the Trapezium light up the gas.

Telescopes and long exposures reveal much more: the dark Horsehead Nebula silhouetted against glowing gas just south of Alnitak, the Flame Nebula beside it, the reflection nebula M78, and Barnard’s Loop, a vast arc of gas wrapping around the whole constellation. Each October, the Orionid meteor shower, debris from Halley’s Comet, appears to radiate from near Betelgeuse.
